document.title: Toronto Notes 2025
document.subtitle: Comprehensive Medical Reference and Review for the MCCQE, 41st edition

questions.question: A 27-year-old motorcyclist is brought to the emergency department after skidding on gravel. His right lower leg is deformed and there is a 4 cm wound over the anterior shin, heavily contaminated with dirt, through which bone is visible. He is hemodynamically stable, distal pulses are palpable and sensation is intact. Radiographs confirm a mid-shaft tibial fracture communicating with the wound. Which of the following is the best initial management?

options.text: Give IV antibiotics immediately, cover the wound with a sterile dressing, splint the limb, give tetanus prophylaxis, and prepare for operative irrigation and debridement
Irrigate and suture the wound closed in the emergency department and discharge on oral antibiotics
Withhold antibiotics until intraoperative cultures have been obtained in the operating room
Apply a circumferential below-knee cast and arrange repeat radiographs in one week
Obtain an MRI of the leg before any wound intervention

questions.explanation: An open fracture is a fractured bone and hematoma in communication with the external or contaminated environment. Emergency measures are ABCs and resuscitation, removal of obvious foreign material, irrigation with normal saline if grossly contaminated, sterile dressings and splinting, immediate IV antibiotics, tetanus toxoid or immunoglobulin as needed, and NPO with preparation for the OR. Operative irrigation and debridement should follow within 6-8 h to decrease the risk of infection.

optionExplanations.b: Contaminated traumatic wounds are debrided in the OR and may be left open to drain, not sutured closed in the emergency department.
optionExplanations.c: Antibiotics are given immediately on arrival; delaying them until cultures are taken increases infection risk.
optionExplanations.d: A circumferential cast does not address the contaminated wound and risks compartment syndrome from a constrictive dressing.
optionExplanations.e: MRI has no role in the emergency management of an open fracture and would delay antibiotics and debridement.

questions.question: A 22-year-old man sustained a closed tibial shaft fracture 8 hours ago and was placed in a below-knee backslab. He now reports severe escalating calf pain that is unrelieved by repeated doses of morphine. The splint has been removed, the limb placed at the level of the heart, and he was re-examined 15 minutes later without improvement. The calf is swollen and tense, passive extension of the toes reproduces severe pain, and the dorsalis pedis pulse is palpable. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Urgent fasciotomy of the leg compartments
Measure intracompartmental pressures and observe the limb if the reading is below 30 mmHg
Elevate the limb well above the level of the heart and reassess in 4 hours
Urgent CT angiography of the lower limb
MRI of the leg to look for muscle necrosis

questions.explanation: Compartment syndrome is a clinical diagnosis: pain out of proportion to the injury is typically the first and most significant symptom, and pain with passive stretch is the most sensitive sign, with a swollen tense compartment. The 5 Ps, including pulselessness, are late signs and must not be awaited. Non-operative measures (removing constrictive dressings, elevating to heart level, re-evaluating every 15 min) have failed here, so urgent fasciotomy is required before irreversible muscle necrosis occurs in 4-6 h.

optionExplanations.b: Pressure monitoring is reserved for children, unconscious patients, or where clinical exam is unreliable; here the clinical picture is diagnostic and measurement would only delay surgery.
optionExplanations.c: Elevation to the level of the heart has already been tried without improvement, and elevating above the heart further reduces perfusion pressure.
optionExplanations.d: A palpable pulse does not exclude compartment syndrome, and angiography delays definitive fasciotomy.
optionExplanations.e: Investigations are usually unnecessary; MRI would waste time within the 4-6 h window before irreversible necrosis.

questions.question: A 58-year-old house painter describes 6 months of right shoulder pain that wakes him at night and prevents him from sleeping on that side. The pain is worst when he reaches overhead, and he has weakness and loss of motion especially between 90 and 130 degrees of abduction. There is tenderness over the greater tuberosity, and passive movement is largely preserved. Radiographs show sclerosis of the undersurface of the acromion. What is the best initial management?

options.text: Physiotherapy with activity modification and non-narcotic analgesia
Immediate arthroscopic acromioplasty and rotator cuff repair
Sling immobilization of the shoulder for 6 weeks
Aspiration of the subacromial bursa for culture

questions.explanation: This is rotator cuff disease with subacromial impingement: insidious onset, night pain, pain worse with active overhead motion with passive movement generally permitted, weakness and loss of ROM especially between 90-130 degrees, and greater tuberosity tenderness. Rotator cuff injury treatment begins with physiotherapy regardless of severity on MRI, together with activity modification and non-narcotic analgesia with or without steroid injection; mild and moderate cases frequently improve.

optionExplanations.b: Surgery is indicated only for severe tear or impingement refractory to 2-3 mo of physiotherapy and 1-2 corticosteroid injections.
optionExplanations.c: Prolonged immobilization is not the treatment and predisposes to secondary adhesive capsulitis.
optionExplanations.d: Arthroplasty is a treatment for advanced glenohumeral arthritis, not for impingement or cuff tendinopathy.
optionExplanations.e: There is no fever or acute inflammatory picture to suggest infection requiring aspiration.

questions.question: A 24-year-old man falls onto his outstretched hand while playing basketball. He has pain on the radial side of the wrist, tenderness in the anatomical snuffbox and over the scaphoid tubercle, and pain with long axis compression into the scaphoid. There is no visible deformity and the wrist is neurovascularly intact. AP, lateral and dedicated scaphoid radiographs taken today are reported as normal. What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Immobilize in a thumb spica cast, treat as a scaphoid fracture, and repeat radiographs in 2 weeks
Diagnose a wrist sprain, apply a tensor bandage, and arrange no follow-up
Proceed directly to ORIF with a headless compression screw
Volar wrist splint for 3 days and return to sport when comfortable

questions.explanation: A scaphoid fracture may not be radiologically evident for up to 2 weeks after acute injury. If a patient has wrist pain and anatomical snuffbox tenderness but a negative x-ray, treat as if positive for a scaphoid fracture and repeat the x-ray 2 weeks later; if the x-ray is still negative, order CT or MRI. Early treatment is critical to outcome given the risk of nonunion and AVN of the proximal pole.

optionExplanations.b: Snuffbox tenderness is 100% sensitive for scaphoid injury; discharging without immobilization risks a missed fracture with nonunion and AVN.
optionExplanations.c: Operative fixation is indicated for displaced, comminuted or humpback deformity fractures or associated perilunate injury, none of which is demonstrated here.
optionExplanations.d: A brief volar splint and early return to sport do not protect an occult scaphoid fracture.
optionExplanations.e: Bone scan is rarely used; the standard pathway is immobilization with repeat x-ray, then CT or MRI if still negative.

questions.question: A 45-year-old warehouse worker develops severe low back pain radiating down both legs after lifting a crate. Over the past 12 hours he has developed numbness of the perineum and buttocks, difficulty initiating urination, and new weakness of ankle dorsiflexion bilaterally. Straight leg raise is positive on both sides and ankle reflexes are diminished. A bladder scan shows a post-void residual volume of 350 mL. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Urgent MRI of the lumbosacral spine with immediate surgical consultation
Six weeks of extension protocol physiotherapy and NSAIDs
Lumbosacral radiographs with outpatient follow-up in 4 weeks
Bed rest with opioid analgesia and reassessment in 72 hours

questions.explanation: Cauda equina syndrome complicates 1-10% of disc herniations and is a surgical emergency. Investigation of disc herniation includes x-ray and MRI, and a post-void residual greater than 100 mL should heighten suspicion for cauda equina syndrome. Saddle anesthesia, bladder dysfunction and progressive neuromotor deficit are back pain red flags; central disc herniation causing cauda equina syndrome is an indication for operative decompression, so urgent MRI and surgical referral are required.

optionExplanations.b: Non-operative symptomatic care applies to uncomplicated disc herniation, not to a patient with saddle anesthesia and urinary retention.
optionExplanations.c: Radiographs alone cannot exclude cauda equina compression and a 4-week delay risks permanent deficit.
optionExplanations.d: Injection does not decompress the cauda equina and delays definitive surgical treatment.
optionExplanations.e: Observation is unsafe: progressive neurological deficit and cauda equina syndrome are indications for surgery.

questions.topic: Cauda Equina Syndrome and Back Pain Red Flags

source.reference: OR28 — Disc Herniation / Low Back Pain Red Flags

questions.question: A 32-year-old restrained driver strikes his flexed right knee on the dashboard in a high-speed collision. Primary and secondary surveys are otherwise unremarkable and he is hemodynamically stable. The right lower limb is shortened, adducted and internally rotated, and any hip movement is exquisitely painful. Distal pulses and sciatic and femoral nerve function are documented as intact. Radiographs show the right femoral head appearing smaller than the left, with no femoral neck fracture. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Urgent closed reduction under conscious sedation or general anesthesia, followed by post-reduction CT
Skeletal traction for 6 weeks with delayed reduction
MRI of the hip before any reduction attempt
Analgesia now with reduction on the next elective operating list

questions.explanation: Posterior hip dislocation is the most frequent type (90%) and is caused by a severe axial load to the knee with the hip flexed and adducted, such as a knee striking the dashboard; the limb is shortened, adducted and internally rotated and the affected femoral head appears smaller on x-ray. Neurovascular status must be examined before reduction, hip dislocations should be reduced within 6 h to decrease the risk of AVN of the femoral head, and post-reduction CT is obtained to assess joint congruity.

optionExplanations.b: Traction with delayed reduction leaves the head dislocated well beyond 6 h and markedly increases AVN risk.
optionExplanations.c: MRI is not required to diagnose the dislocation and would delay urgent reduction; CT is obtained after reduction.
optionExplanations.d: Arthroplasty is not the acute treatment of a simple dislocation without femoral neck fracture.
optionExplanations.e: Delaying reduction to an elective list forfeits the 6 h window that reduces the risk of avascular necrosis.

questions.question: An 82-year-old woman with osteoporosis falls from standing height onto her left side. She has acute left hip pain, is unable to weight-bear, and the left leg is shortened and externally rotated with painful range of motion. Radiographs of the hip and pelvis, including a cross table lateral view, show a displaced intracapsular subcapital fracture of the femoral neck with disruption of Shenton's line. Which complication is she at greatest risk of as a direct consequence of this fracture location?

options.text: Avascular necrosis of the femoral head
Varus displacement of the proximal fragment typical of extracapsular fractures

questions.explanation: A subcapital femoral neck fracture is intracapsular, and complications listed for this fracture type are DVT, nonunion and AVN. The blood supply runs distal to proximal along the femoral neck to the head via the medial and lateral femoral circumflex arteries, so it is susceptible to AVN when disrupted; femoral neck fracture is a listed cause of AVN of the femoral head, along with chronic steroid use, SCFE and Legg-Calve-Perthes disease.

optionExplanations.b: Varus displacement of the proximal fragment is a complication of extracapsular intertrochanteric fractures, not intracapsular subcapital fractures.
optionExplanations.c: Volkmann ischemic contracture follows compartment syndrome of the forearm, especially after supracondylar humerus and both bone forearm fractures.
optionExplanations.d: Sciatic nerve palsy is characteristically associated with hip dislocation rather than with a femoral neck fracture.
optionExplanations.e: Compartment syndrome typically involves fibro-osseous compartments such as the calf or forearm, not an intracapsular hip fracture.

questions.question: A 20-year-old university soccer player plants her foot and pivots sharply to change direction. She feels and hears a pop in her right knee, is unable to continue playing, and the knee swells within an hour. She reports the knee giving way when she tries to walk. On examination there is a tense effusion, and with the knee flexed to 90 degrees and the foot immobilized the tibia can be subluxed anteriorly on the femur. Which structure has most likely been injured?
questions.explanation: The most common ACL mechanism is non-contact sudden deceleration with a change of direction or landing manoeuvre, producing anterior tibial translation with valgus knee stress. The history of an audible pop, immediate swelling, the knee giving way and inability to continue activity, with effusion (hemarthrosis) and a positive anterior drawer, fits ACL rupture; ACL tears are much more common than PCL tears.

optionExplanations.b: PCL injury follows hyperflexion, hyperextension, or a posteriorly directed blow to the flexed knee such as a dashboard injury, and produces a positive posterior drawer.
optionExplanations.c: MCL tears result from a valgus force with laxity on valgus stress testing rather than anterior tibial subluxation.
optionExplanations.d: Meniscal tears typically follow a twisting force on the partially flexed knee, with effusion of insidious onset over 24-48 h and joint line tenderness.
optionExplanations.e: Patellar tendon rupture presents with inability to extend the knee, a palpable gap, and a high riding patella, not anterior tibial subluxation.

questions.question: A 28-year-old man twists his left knee while stepping down from a truck and turning. Swelling developed gradually over the following 36 hours. He describes clicking and increased pain with squatting and twisting. Examination reveals a moderate effusion and medial joint line tenderness, and pain with a palpable click when the joint line is palpated during knee flexion and extension. He cannot fully extend the knee and there is a firm mechanical block to passive extension. Radiographs show no fracture. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Arrange urgent arthroscopy for repair or partial meniscectomy
NSAIDs with a range of motion and strengthening program
Knee immobilizer for 4 weeks and then reassess
Outpatient MRI in 6 weeks with interim activity modification
Aspiration of the effusion and intra-articular corticosteroid injection

questions.explanation: The mechanism (twisting force on a partially flexed knee such as stepping down and turning), effusion of insidious onset 24-48 h after injury, joint line tenderness and locking indicate a meniscal tear. A locked knee, in which the patient cannot fully extend the knee because of a mechanical block, is a surgical emergency; arthroscopic repair or partial meniscectomy is indicated, and repair is generally preferred in younger patients with traumatic, non-degenerative tears.

optionExplanations.b: Non-operative range of motion and strengthening is indicated when the knee is not locked or for degenerative tears with osteoarthritis.
optionExplanations.c: Immobilization does not relieve a mechanical block and delays urgent surgical treatment of a locked knee.
optionExplanations.d: A locked knee cannot wait 6 weeks for imaging; operative treatment is indicated urgently.
optionExplanations.e: Aspiration and steroid injection do not remove the displaced meniscal fragment obstructing extension.

questions.question: A 30-year-old woman inverts her right ankle stepping off a curb and is seen 2 hours later. She has pain in the malleolar zone and has been able to limp four steps in the emergency department. On palpation there is bony tenderness over the posterior edge and tip of the lateral malleolus. The medial malleolus is not tender, and there is no midfoot pain and no tenderness over the navicular or the base of the fifth metatarsal. What is the most appropriate imaging?

options.text: AP, mortise and lateral radiographs of the ankle
No imaging; manage as a lateral ligament sprain
Ultrasound of the lateral collateral ligaments

questions.explanation: The Ottawa Ankle and Foot Rules, which have nearly 100% sensitivity, should guide x-ray use: ankle films are required for pain in the malleolar zone plus bony tenderness over the posterior edge or tip of either malleolus, or inability to weight bear both immediately and in the emergency department. This patient has malleolar zone pain with tenderness at the tip of the lateral malleolus, so ankle radiographs are indicated: AP, mortise and lateral views, the mortise view being taken at 15 degrees of internal rotation to give a true view of the joint.

optionExplanations.b: The Ottawa ankle rule is positive because of bony tenderness at the lateral malleolus, so radiographs cannot be omitted.
optionExplanations.c: MRI is not the initial imaging modality for a suspected ankle fracture.
optionExplanations.d: Ultrasound is not used to guide initial imaging decisions in acute ankle trauma.
optionExplanations.e: Foot films are indicated for midfoot zone pain with navicular or fifth metatarsal base tenderness, which she does not have.

questions.topic: Ottawa Ankle Rules and Ankle Injury Imaging

source.reference: OR41 — Evaluation of Ankle and Foot Complaints

questions.question: A 13-year-old boy with obesity presents with 6 weeks of dull right knee and anterior thigh pain and a limp. There is no history of trauma. The knee has no effusion, no joint line tenderness and full painless motion. Examination of the right hip shows restricted internal rotation, abduction and flexion, with obligatory external rotation of the hip during passive flexion. There is a positive Trendelenburg sign on the right. He is afebrile and able to walk with crutches. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: SCFE is the most common adolescent hip disorder, peaking at the pubertal growth spurt, with obesity as the number one risk factor and male sex a further risk. Chronic presentations give groin and anterior thigh pain that may present as knee pain through activation of the medial obturator nerve, with a positive Trendelenburg sign, restricted internal rotation, abduction and flexion, and the Drehmann sign of obligatory external rotation during passive hip flexion. Ability to bear weight with crutches makes this a stable slip.

optionExplanations.b: Legg-Calve-Perthes disease presents at 4-8 years of age, much younger than this patient.
optionExplanations.c: Transient synovitis does not produce a 6-week history with the Drehmann sign, and the Kocher criteria are used to distinguish it from a septic joint.
optionExplanations.d: Septic arthritis progresses over hours with fever and inability to weight bear, not a 6-week afebrile course.
optionExplanations.e: Osgood-Schlatter disease causes a tender lump over the tibial tuberosity with pain on resisted leg extension, and does not restrict hip motion.

questions.question: A 3-month-old girl born in frank breech presentation is assessed because her mother noticed asymmetry of the legs. She is a first-born child and there is a family history of childhood hip problems. Examination shows limited abduction of the flexed left hip, asymmetric thigh skin folds, and a palpable clunk felt with the fingertips as the left hip is abducted. Ultrasound confirms a shallow acetabulum with a reducible dislocated left femoral head. What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Pavlik harness to maintain hip abduction and flexion
Closed reduction under general anesthesia with hip spica casting
Observation with repeat clinical examination at 2 years of age

questions.explanation: Developmental dysplasia of the hip is the most common orthopedic disorder in newborns; risk factors include family history, female sex, frank breech, first born and left hip involvement. Diagnosis is clinical, with limited abduction of the flexed hip, skin fold asymmetry, and a palpable clunk on Ortolani's test indicating a reducible hip. From 0-6 months the treatment is to reduce the hip using a Pavlik harness to maintain abduction and flexion.

optionExplanations.b: Reduction under general anesthesia with a hip spica cast is used from 6-18 months, or earlier only if the Pavlik harness fails.
optionExplanations.c: Open reduction with spica casting is reserved for children aged 18 months to 2 years.
optionExplanations.d: Pelvic and/or femoral osteotomy is used after 2 years of age.
optionExplanations.e: Untreated dysplasia does not correct itself, and delaying to age 2 commits the child to osteotomy.

source.reference: OR47 — Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip

questions.question: A 24-year-old man is in hospital after high energy trauma in an MVC, with closed femoral and tibial fractures. Thirty-six hours later he develops SOB and a decreased level of consciousness. Oxygen saturation is 85%, a petechial rash is seen over the chest, and platelets have fallen to 78 x 10^9/L. There is no hypotension or hypovolemia and hemoglobin is unchanged. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Pulmonary embolism from a deep vein thrombosis
Sepsis from a missed open fracture

questions.explanation: Complications of the trauma patient include hemorrhage, fat embolism syndrome, venous thromboembolism (DVT and PE), neurological and vascular damage, and sepsis and/or tetanus infection especially if a missed open fracture. Fat embolism syndrome is characterized by SOB, hypoxemia, petechial rash, thrombocytopenia and neurological symptoms, and all of these features are present here after high energy trauma with long bone fractures. Hemorrhage is the life-threatening complication that produces signs and symptoms of hypovolemic shock, which this patient does not have.

optionExplanations.a: Venous thromboembolism causes dyspnea and hypoxemia but does not explain the petechial rash and thrombocytopenia.
optionExplanations.c: Hemorrhage produces signs and symptoms of hypovolemic shock; his blood pressure and hemoglobin are stable.
optionExplanations.d: Sepsis from a missed open fracture is a recognized complication, but both fractures are closed and there is no source or fever described.
optionExplanations.e: Tetanus is described as a complication of missed open fractures and does not cause hypoxemia with a petechial rash.

source.reference: OR9 — Orthopedic Emergencies: Trauma Patient Workup

questions.question: A 62-year-old man presents with 2 days of acute onset monoarticular knee pain and refusal to bear weight. His temperature is 38.6 C. The knee is erythematous, warm and swollen, with pain on both active and passive range of motion. WBC, ESR and CRP are elevated and blood cultures have been drawn. Knee x-ray shows no fracture, tumour or metabolic bone disease. What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Joint aspiration for cell count, crystals, Gram stain and culture and sensitivity
Bone scan of the lower limbs

questions.explanation: An acutely painful, erythematous, warm, swollen joint with pain on active and passive ROM, fever and inability to bear weight is investigated with x-ray, inflammatory markers and blood cultures plus joint aspirate. The aspirate in septic arthritis is cloudy yellow with WBC greater than 50000 and more than 90% neutrophils, protein above 4.4 mg/dL, joint glucose below 60% of blood glucose, no crystals and a positive Gram stain. Empiric IV antibiotics are then adjusted according to the aspirate culture and sensitivity results.

optionExplanations.b: MRI is not part of the described workup and would delay the aspirate needed to confirm infection and guide antibiotics.
optionExplanations.c: A serum uric acid level does not distinguish infection from crystal disease; the aspirate is examined for crystals directly.
optionExplanations.d: A bone scan adds nothing acutely and does not provide fluid for Gram stain and culture.
optionExplanations.e: The x-ray has already served its purpose of ruling out fracture, tumour and metabolic bone disease; repeating it delays diagnosis.

questions.question: A 35-year-old man falls and injures his right arm. Radiographs show a transverse fracture of the middle third of the humeral shaft with 20 degrees of varus angulation and 1 cm of shortening. The skin is intact. He has a drop wrist with sensory impairment over the dorsum of the hand. The radial pulse is normal, the forearm is soft and the forearm bones are uninjured. What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Hanging cast with collar and cuff sling until swelling subsides, then a Sarmiento functional brace
Urgent surgical exploration and repair of the radial nerve
ORIF with plate fixation of the humeral shaft

questions.explanation: In general humeral shaft fractures are treated non-operatively, and the acceptable deformities for non-operative treatment are less than 20 degrees of anterior angulation, less than 30 degrees of varus angulation and less than 3 cm of shortening, since compensatory shoulder ROM tolerates residual deformity. This fracture is within those limits, so a hanging cast followed by a Sarmiento functional brace is appropriate. Radial nerve palsy accompanying a humeral shaft fracture is expected to recover spontaneously in 3-4 months, with EMG reserved for those that do not.

optionExplanations.b: A radial nerve palsy with a closed humeral shaft fracture is expected to recover spontaneously in 3-4 months, with EMG if it does not; exploration is not the first move.
optionExplanations.c: Plating is the most common operative option but is reserved for the NO CAST indications, pathological fracture or a floating elbow, none of which is present.
optionExplanations.d: Intramedullary rod insertion is an operative alternative and carries the same requirement for an operative indication.
optionExplanations.e: External fixation of the humeral shaft is rare and is not indicated for a closed fracture with acceptable alignment.

questions.question: A 7-year-old boy falls off the monkey bars onto an outstretched hand. His elbow is swollen and tender with ecchymosis and dimpling of the skin in the antecubital fossa. He cannot perform the a-ok sign and reports numbness in the volar aspect of the first three digits. The radial pulse is present. Radiographs show a displaced extension-type fracture proximal to the capitulum and trochlea, with disruption of the anterior humeral line. What is the most appropriate treatment?

options.text: Closed reduction with percutaneous pinning, followed by a limb cast with the elbow flexed less than 90 degrees
Closed reduction with a long arm plaster slab in 90 degrees of flexion for 3 weeks
Collar and cuff sling with early range of motion
Open reduction and internal fixation with plates and screws

questions.explanation: Supracondylar fractures are most common in the pediatric population, over 96% are extension injuries from a FOOSH, and median nerve injury is commonly associated with the extension type. Non-operative treatment with a long arm plaster slab applies only to nondisplaced type 1 fractures; displacement greater than 50%, vascular injury or an open fracture are operative indications. Treatment is closed reduction plus percutaneous pinning followed by a limb cast with the elbow flexed less than 90 degrees.

optionExplanations.b: A long arm plaster slab in 90 degrees of flexion is reserved for the nondisplaced pediatric type 1 supracondylar fracture.
optionExplanations.c: A sling does not maintain reduction of a displaced supracondylar fracture and risks cubitus varus malalignment.
optionExplanations.d: ORIF is necessary in adults; children are managed with closed reduction and percutaneous pinning.
optionExplanations.e: Total elbow arthroplasty is an option for complex bicolumnar distal humerus fractures in the elderly, not for a child.

questions.question: A 6-year-old girl falls onto a hyperextended elbow. She has pain, swelling and decreased rotation of the forearm, with a palpable lump at the radial head. Radiographs of the elbow, wrist and forearm show a fracture of the proximal third of the ulna angled apex anterior, with the radial head dislocated anteriorly. The distal radioulnar joint is intact. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Combined radius and ulna shaft fracture

questions.explanation: A Monteggia fracture is a fracture of the proximal ulna with radial head dislocation and proximal radioulnar joint injury, classically from a fall on the hyperextended elbow, a direct blow to the posterior forearm or hyperpronation. The typical deformity is an ulna angled apex anterior with the radial head dislocated anteriorly, and the injury is more common with a better prognosis in the pediatric age group. Posterior interosseous nerve injury is the most common associated nerve injury and is observed for 3 months as most resolve spontaneously.

optionExplanations.b: A Galeazzi fracture is a fracture of the distal radial shaft with disruption of the DRUJ, which is intact here.
optionExplanations.c: A nightstick fracture is an isolated ulnar fracture without dislocation of the radial head.
optionExplanations.d: A combined radius and ulna shaft fracture involves both shafts without radial head dislocation.
optionExplanations.e: The radial head dislocation here is accompanied by a proximal ulna fracture, so it is not an isolated dislocation.

questions.question: A 68-year-old woman with osteoporotic bone falls onto an outstretched hand. She has a dinner fork deformity of the wrist with swelling, ecchymosis and tenderness, and a normal neurovascular examination. Radiographs show an extra-articular transverse distal radius fracture about 2 cm proximal to the radiocarpal joint, with dorsal displacement and an ulnar styloid fracture. There is no intra-articular extension. What is the best initial treatment?

options.text: Hematoma block with closed reduction and application of a dorsal slab or below elbow cast
Percutaneous pinning of the distal radius
Sling immobilization alone with early range of motion

questions.explanation: This is a Colles fracture, the most common fracture in those over 40 yr, especially women and those with osteoporotic bone. Initial treatment is non-operative: a hematoma block or conscious sedation, closed reduction by traction with extension then traction with ulnar deviation, pronation and flexion of the distal fragment, and a dorsal slab or below elbow cast for 5-6 wk, with post-reduction films obtained immediately. Percutaneous pinning, external fixation or ORIF are reserved for failed closed reduction or loss of reduction.

optionExplanations.b: ORIF is indicated for failed closed reduction or loss of reduction, not as the initial treatment of an extra-articular fracture.
optionExplanations.c: Percutaneous pinning is an operative option used after closed reduction fails.
optionExplanations.d: External fixation is likewise reserved for failed or lost reduction.
optionExplanations.e: A dorsally displaced fracture requires reduction and casting; a sling alone will not restore radial height, inclination or volar tilt.

questions.question: A 42-year-old man has 3 weeks of leg dominant pain radiating down the lateral aspect of the leg. On examination he has weakness of extensor hallucis longus and of hip abduction, numbness over the first dorsal webspace and the lateral leg, and he cannot heel walk. Knee and ankle reflexes are normal. Straight leg raise reproduces his symptoms. Which nerve root is most likely involved?
questions.explanation: The L5 root supplies extensor hallucis longus and gluteus medius (hip abduction), gives sensation to the first dorsal webspace and lateral leg, and is screened by heel walking, with the medial hamstring reflex and a positive straight leg raise. L4 would give quadriceps and tibialis anterior weakness with medial malleolus numbness, a lost knee reflex and a positive femoral stretch test, and S1 would give weak plantar flexion, lateral foot numbness and a lost ankle reflex.

optionExplanations.a: An L3 lesion would not produce the extensor hallucis longus and hip abduction weakness with first dorsal webspace numbness described.
optionExplanations.b: L4 involvement causes knee extension and ankle dorsiflexion weakness, medial malleolus numbness and loss of the knee reflex, none of which is present.
optionExplanations.d: S1 involvement causes weak ankle plantar flexion and eversion, lateral foot numbness and a lost ankle reflex; his ankle reflex is normal.
optionExplanations.e: S2 is not the root tested by heel walking or by first dorsal webspace sensation.

questions.question: A 71-year-old man describes bilateral back and leg pain brought on by standing and walking. The pain eases when he sits or leans forward over a shopping cart, with relief taking about 10 minutes, and the distance he can walk varies from day to day. He has mild motor weakness in both legs. Pedal pulses are normal and symmetric. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Spinal stenosis is narrowing of the spinal canal and presents with bilateral back and leg pain, neurogenic claudication and possible motor weakness. Neurogenic claudication is aggravated by standing and walking with a variable walking distance, is alleviated by a change in position such as flexion, sitting or lying down, and takes about 10 min to settle, whereas vascular claudication is reproducible with exercise and relieved within 2 min of stopping. CT or MRI demonstrating narrowing of the spinal canal confirms the diagnosis.

optionExplanations.b: Vascular claudication is reproducible for a set walking distance, relieved in about 2 min by stopping, and would not be relieved simply by leaning forward; his pulses are normal.
optionExplanations.c: Mechanical back pain is back dominant pain without nerve impingement and without neurological signs.
optionExplanations.d: Degenerative disc disease causes axial back pain worse with axial loading and flexion, not pain relieved by flexion.
optionExplanations.e: Lumbar disc herniation typically gives back or leg dominant pain with tenderness between spinous processes and a positional flexion injury history, not positional claudication.

questions.question: A 46-year-old man is struck by a car. His left knee is grossly unstable and deformed with a large effusion and severe pain. The foot is cool, the dorsalis pedis pulse is diminished and the ABI is 0.6. He has a foot drop. Radiographs show posterior displacement of the tibia relative to the femur with an avulsion of the fibular head. What is the next best step in management?

options.text: Urgent closed reduction and immobilization, with reassessment of neurovascular status
CT angiogram of the limb before any attempt at reduction
Immediate multiligament reconstruction in the operating room
Application of a hinged knee brace with serial ABI measurements
MRI of the knee to define the pattern of ligamentous injury

questions.explanation: A dislocated knee is by definition caused by tears of multiple ligaments and may present with an ischemic limb, neurological deficit or compartment syndrome. Treatment begins with urgent closed reduction and immobilization, followed by assessment and management of neurovascular injuries and compartment syndrome; an abnormal vascular exam or ABI below 0.9 then prompts arteriogram or CT angiogram, and emergent operative repair is indicated for vascular injury, open injury, an irreducible or grossly unstable dislocation, or compartment syndrome. Ligament reconstruction is typically performed in a delayed fashion.

optionExplanations.b: Angiography is obtained after reduction; delaying reduction of an ischemic dislocated knee to image first prolongs the ischemia.
optionExplanations.c: Ligament reconstruction to restore knee stability is typically performed in a delayed fashion, not at initial presentation.
optionExplanations.d: Bracing and observation ignore the ischemic limb, which requires reduction and vascular assessment.
optionExplanations.e: MRI does not address the vascular emergency and would delay reduction.

questions.question: A 38-year-old roofer falls 4 m from a ladder and lands on both heels. Both heels are swollen and exquisitely tender and he cannot walk. He also reports discomfort in his lower back. Radiographs of both feet show bilateral intra-articular calcaneal fractures. Distal pulses and sensation are intact and the compartments are soft. Which additional investigation is most appropriate?

options.text: Radiographs of the thoracic and lumbar spine

questions.explanation: Calcaneal fractures are caused by high energy axial loading, typically a fall from height onto the heels, and 10% are associated with compression fractures of the thoracic or lumbar spine, so spine injury must be ruled out. With a history of significant trauma from axial loading of the lower limb, spinal injuries and talar or calcaneal fractures should all be considered. His back discomfort makes thoracolumbar imaging the priority.

optionExplanations.b: The Canale view is used to image a suspected talar fracture, and the calcaneal fractures are already confirmed.
optionExplanations.c: MRI does not add to management here; CT is the modality used to assess intra-articular extension of calcaneal fractures.
optionExplanations.d: There is no clinical suggestion of an Achilles injury, and this would miss the associated spine fracture.
optionExplanations.e: A bone scan does not evaluate the thoracolumbar spine acutely and adds nothing to a radiographically confirmed fracture.

questions.question: A 44-year-old recreational squash player felt sudden pain and heard an audible pop at the back of the ankle while pushing off. He cannot plantarflex against resistance and has an apprehensive toe off when walking. There is a palpable gap about 4 cm above the insertion on the heel. With the patient prone, squeezing the calf produces no plantar flexion. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Achilles tendon rupture follows sudden forced plantar flexion or violent dorsiflexion during stop-and-go sports such as squash, tennis and basketball, and presents with an audible pop, sudden pain with push-off, inability to plantarflex, a palpable gap and apprehensive toe off. Absence of passive plantar flexion when the calf is squeezed with the patient prone is a positive Thompson test, indicating a ruptured tendon. The most common site of rupture is 2-6 cm from the insertion, where the blood supply is poorest.

optionExplanations.b: Achilles tendonitis causes chronic posterior heel pain, swelling and a thickened tendon, without a palpable gap or a positive Thompson test.
optionExplanations.c: Retrocalcaneal bursitis presents as a painful heel bump associated with chronic tendonitis, not an acute pop with loss of plantar flexion.
optionExplanations.d: A Haglund deformity is a painful bony heel bump, and passive plantar flexion on calf squeeze would be preserved.
optionExplanations.e: A calcaneal fracture follows high energy axial loading onto the heel and would show marked heel swelling and bony injury on x-ray.

questions.question: A 7-month-old infant who is not yet walking is brought in with a swollen, painful right thigh. The caregiver states the infant rolled off a couch onto a carpeted floor. Radiographs show a right femur fracture, a metaphyseal corner fracture of the distal tibia, and healing posterior rib fractures at different stages of healing. The infant is otherwise well and hemodynamically stable. What is the next best step in management?

options.text: Admit the child to hospital, contact the appropriate authorities, engage social work, and treat the injuries as normal
Apply a hip spica cast and discharge home with outpatient orthopedic follow-up
Reassure the caregiver that the stated mechanism explains the injuries and discharge
Splint the limb and repeat radiographs in 2 weeks before deciding on further action
Treat the femur fracture and arrange routine community follow-up without further inquiry

questions.explanation: In children the clinician must always consider non-accidental injury and confirm that the stated mechanism is compatible with the injury presentation, with a high index of suspicion for fractures in non-ambulating children under 1 yr and for x-ray evidence of healing fractures at different sites and different stages of healing. A metaphyseal corner fracture is the hallmark of non-accidental trauma, and a femur fracture under 1 yr and posterior rib fractures are also suspicious. When non-accidental injury is suspected, admit the child to hospital, contact the appropriate authorities, engage allied health such as social work, and treat the injuries as normal.

optionExplanations.b: Discharging the infant home returns the child to a potentially unsafe environment despite hallmark features of non-accidental trauma.
optionExplanations.c: A low energy roll off a couch is not compatible with a femur fracture, a metaphyseal corner fracture and healing posterior rib fractures in a non-ambulating infant.
optionExplanations.d: Fractures at different sites and stages of healing are already documented; delaying protection of the child is unsafe.
optionExplanations.e: Treating only the fracture omits the mandatory reporting and multidisciplinary response required for suspected non-accidental injury.

questions.question: A 13-year-old boy who plays competitive basketball has 3 months of anterior knee pain exacerbated by jumping and kneeling and relieved by rest. There is a tender lump over the tibial tuberosity and pain on resisted leg extension. There is no effusion, no warmth and no fever, and the knee is stable. Lateral knee x-ray shows fragmentation of the tibial tubercle. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Osgood-Schlatter disease is inflammation of the patellar ligament at its insertion on the tibial tuberosity, caused by repetitive tensile stress producing a minor avulsion and tibial tubercle apophysitis, and it affects boys 12-15 yr more than girls. It presents with a tender lump over the tibial tuberosity, pain on resisted leg extension and anterior knee pain exacerbated by jumping or kneeling and relieved by rest, with lateral knee x-ray showing fragmentation of the tibial tubercle. It is a benign, self-limited condition managed by avoiding aggravating activities such as basketball, plus NSAIDs, rest and strengthening.

optionExplanations.b: A patellar tendon rupture causes acute inability to extend the knee, not months of activity-related pain with a tender tubercle.
optionExplanations.c: Septic arthritis would present with fever, an erythematous warm swollen joint and pain on passive motion.
optionExplanations.d: Osteochondritis dissecans is avascular necrosis of subchondral bone and would not produce a tender lump at the tibial tuberosity with tubercle fragmentation.
optionExplanations.e: A malignant bone tumour causes progressive night pain with a soft tissue mass and aggressive radiographic features, which are absent here.

questions.question: A 16-year-old boy has 3 months of progressive pain around the right knee that is worse at night, with poorly defined swelling and decreased range of motion. Radiographs of the distal femur show a destructive blastic lesion with a sunburst pattern, periosteal reaction lifting the cortex off the bone, and an adjacent soft tissue mass. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The majority of osteosarcomas occur in the 2nd decade of life and have a predilection for sites of rapid growth, most often the distal femur, followed by the proximal tibia and proximal humerus. It causes progressive pain, night pain, poorly defined swelling and decreased ROM, and radiographs show a characteristic blastic and destructive lesion with a sunburst pattern, periosteal reaction (Codman's triangle) and a soft tissue mass. Staging includes a bone scan for skeletal metastases and CT chest for pulmonary metastases before neo-adjuvant chemotherapy and limb salvage resection.

optionExplanations.b: Ewing's sarcoma occurs between ages 5-25 yr but gives a moth-eaten destructive lesion with onion-skinning and often mimics infection with fever, erythema and raised inflammatory markers.
optionExplanations.c: Chondrosarcoma typically arises after age 40 in primary cases and shows irregular popcorn calcification in the medullary cavity.
optionExplanations.d: Multiple myeloma occurs in 90% of cases after age 40 and produces multiple punched-out lesions without surrounding sclerosis.
optionExplanations.e: Metastatic carcinoma is the common bone lesion of adults over 40 yr and would be unusual in a 16-year-old.

questions.question: A 24-year-old rugby player is tackled and falls onto the point of his left shoulder with the arm adducted. He has pain on adduction of the shoulder and on palpation over the acromioclavicular joint, limited range of motion, and a palpable step deformity between the distal clavicle and the acromion. Neurovascular examination of the limb is normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Medial physeal fracture of the clavicle

questions.explanation: Acromioclavicular joint pathology is subluxation or dislocation of the AC joint, and the mechanism is a fall onto the shoulder with an adducted arm or direct trauma to the point of the shoulder. The clinical features given by the source are pain with adduction of the shoulder and/or palpation over the AC joint, limited ROM, and a palpable step deformity between the distal clavicle and the acromion with dislocation (piano key sign). This patient has that exact mechanism and that exact triad, so the AC joint, not the clavicle shaft, is the injured structure.

optionExplanations.b: Middle-third fractures account for 80% of clavicle fractures but present with pain and tenting of the skin over the clavicle, with the arm clasped to the chest, rather than a step between the distal clavicle and acromion.
optionExplanations.c: A distal-third clavicle fracture also produces lateral shoulder pain, but tenderness and deformity are over the clavicle itself; the step deformity at the AC joint indicates disruption of the AC and CC ligaments.
optionExplanations.d: Sternoclavicular injury involves the medial end of the clavicle and is assessed with CT; it would not produce a step deformity between the distal clavicle and the acromion.
optionExplanations.e: Medial physeal fractures of the clavicle occur at the medial end and are also a CT indication; they do not explain lateral pain with adduction and an AC joint step.

questions.question: A 38-year-old man falls onto his outstretched hand with the elbow extended and the forearm pronated. He has marked local tenderness over the radial head at the lateral elbow and pain on pronation and supination. X-ray shows a displaced radial head fracture with 4 mm of joint incongruity and a posterior fat pad. On examination there is a mechanical block to forearm rotation. What is the most appropriate treatment?

options.text: Elbow slab or sling for 3-5 days with early range of motion
Cast immobilization with the elbow at 90 degrees of flexion for 6 weeks
Radial head excision without prosthetic replacement

questions.explanation: Radial head fractures are treated by Mason class. A displaced fracture of 2 mm or more is Mason class 2, and ORIF is indicated if angulation is greater than 30 degrees, at least one third of the radial head is involved, at least 3 mm of joint incongruity exists, or there is a block to forearm rotation. ORIF remains the gold standard for Mason class 2 and above. This patient has 4 mm of joint incongruity plus a mechanical block to rotation, so ORIF is indicated.

optionExplanations.a: An elbow slab or sling for 3-5 days with early ROM is the treatment for a Mason class 1 nondisplaced fracture of less than 2 mm, not for a displaced fracture with a block to rotation.
optionExplanations.c: Radial head excision with a prosthesis is reserved for comminuted fractures (Mason class 3 and 4) or when ORIF is not feasible; this fracture is displaced but reconstructable.
optionExplanations.d: Six weeks of cast immobilization causes stiffness — the elbow should not be immobilized beyond 2-3 weeks — and it would not correct the articular incongruity or the mechanical block.
optionExplanations.e: Excising the radial head without replacing it risks recurrent instability if the MCL is injured, and it does not restore joint congruity in a fracture amenable to fixation.

questions.question: A 54-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes reports 4 months of gradual onset diffuse right shoulder pain that is worse at night and prevents her sleeping on that side. There was no injury and no period of immobilization. On examination both active and passive range of motion are decreased in all planes. AP, scapular Y, and axillary x-rays of the shoulder are normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Cervical disc disease with referred shoulder pain

questions.explanation: Adhesive capsulitis is progressive pain and stiffness of the shoulder with gradual onset over weeks to months, decreased active AND passive ROM, and pain worse at night that often prevents sleeping on the affected side. Primary adhesive capsulitis is idiopathic and often associated with DM, whereas secondary disease follows prolonged immobilization, MI, stroke, or shoulder trauma. This diabetic patient has the typical picture with no antecedent immobilization or trauma, and x-ray may be normal in this disorder.

optionExplanations.b: Rotator cuff pathology limits active elevation while passive ROM is preserved; loss of both active and passive motion points to capsular contracture rather than tendon disease.
optionExplanations.c: Proximal humeral fracture follows high energy trauma in the young or a FOOSH from standing height in osteoporotic elderly, with tenderness, deformity, swelling, and bruising down the arm and chest; this patient had no injury and normal x-rays.
optionExplanations.d: Shoulder-hand syndrome is a form of secondary adhesive capsulitis characterized by arm and shoulder pain with diffuse swelling, and follows prolonged immobilization or events such as MI or stroke, none of which is present.
optionExplanations.e: Cervical disc disease is listed as a condition associated with increased incidence of adhesive capsulitis, but referred pain from the neck would not produce loss of passive glenohumeral motion.

questions.question: A 34-year-old man strikes his knee on the dashboard in a motor vehicle collision. He has marked tenderness over the patella and a tense effusion. He can perform a straight leg raise and extend the knee against gravity. AP, lateral, and skyline x-rays show a transverse patellar fracture with a 1 mm articular step-off and 2 mm of fragment separation, with no comminution. What is the best initial treatment?

options.text: Straight leg immobilization in a removable brace with weight bearing as tolerated
Open reduction and internal fixation of the patella
Immediate quadriceps strengthening physiotherapy without immobilization

questions.explanation: Non-operative treatment of a patellar fracture is indicated when the fracture is non or minimally displaced, with a step-off less than 2-3 mm and a fracture gap less than 1-4 mm, or when the extensor mechanism is intact. That treatment is straight leg immobilization for 1-4 wk in a removable brace or splint with weight bearing as tolerated, progressing in flexion after 2-3 wk. This man has a 1 mm step-off, 2 mm separation, no comminution, and an intact extensor mechanism, so he falls below the operative thresholds.

optionExplanations.b: ORIF is indicated for a step-off greater than 2 mm, fragment separation greater than 3 mm, comminution, a disrupted extensor mechanism, or an open fracture, none of which this patient has.
optionExplanations.c: Partial patellectomy is reserved for comminuted fractures managed operatively, not a minimally displaced transverse fracture.
optionExplanations.d: Complete patellectomy is a salvage option for severe comminution during operative management and is not appropriate when the fracture meets non-operative criteria.
optionExplanations.e: Quadriceps strengthening physiotherapy is started only once pain has subsided and after the initial period of straight leg immobilization; starting immediately risks loss of reduction.
